resources.string: Me gustaría: I would like (a polite wish)
Verb like gustar: the thing liked is the subject (me gusta el café = coffee pleases me = I like coffee)
A feeling about something: the next verb is in the subjunctive (me alegra que estés aquí = I’m glad you’re here)
Tener que: have to, must
Hay que: one has to, it’s necessary to (said of nobody in particular)
Vamos a: let’s…, or we’re going to…
Ir a + infinitive: going to (a plan, or the near future)
Estar + gerund: happening right now, or at that moment (estoy comiendo = I’m eating)
Seguir + gerund: still doing, keep doing
Llevar + time + gerund: have been doing for (llevo dos horas esperando = I’ve been waiting for two hours)
Ir + gerund: little by little (andar + gerund: going around doing)
Poder: can, be able to, may
Querer + infinitive: want to
Deber: should, must (debería = ought to)
Soler: usually do (suelo = I usually; solía = I used to)
Acabar de: have just done (acabo de llegar = I’ve just arrived)
Volver a: do again
Start to (empezar a, comenzar a; ponerse a = suddenly start)
Dejar de: stop doing (no dejes de = don’t fail to)
About to do something
Hacer falta: be needed (me hace falta = I need)
Tener + noun: to be (tengo hambre = I’m hungry; tengo veinte años = I’m twenty)
Present perfect: have done (he comido = I have eaten), often for today or this week
Pluperfect: had done (before another past moment)
Future perfect: will have done; also a guess about the past (habrá salido = he must have gone out)
Conditional perfect: would have done
Perfect subjunctive: have done, where the subjunctive is needed (espero que hayas dormido bien)
Pluperfect subjunctive: had done, in wishes and unreal pasts (ojalá hubiera sabido = if only I had known)
Passive: is / was done (by someone: por)
Estar + participle: a state that results from something (está cerrada = it’s closed)
Wanting or asking someone else to do something: the next verb is in the subjunctive (quiero que vengas = I want you to come)
It’s important / possible / better that…: the next verb is in the subjunctive
Doubt or denial: the next verb is in the subjunctive (no creo que venga = I don’t think he’ll come)
Ojalá: I hope, if only (+ subjunctive: ojalá llueva)
Para que: so that (+ subjunctive)
Antes de que: before (+ subjunctive)
Unless, without, as long as, in case: always + subjunctive
Como si: as if (+ imperfect subjunctive: como si fuera = as if he were)
Maybe (quizás and tal vez often take the subjunctive; a lo mejor takes the indicative)
Ser: to be: who or what something is, where it’s from, what it’s like, the time (es médica, son las tres)
Estar: to be: where something is, or how it is right now (estoy cansado = I’m tired)
Hay: there is, there are (había = there was, there were)
¡Qué…!: How…! What a…! (¡qué bonito! = how beautiful!)
Por qué: why (porque, one word, = because)
Question word: always written with an accent (¿dónde?, ¿cómo?, ¿qué?), also inside a sentence (no sé dónde está)
¿Verdad? / ¿no?: …, right? (asks the listener to agree)
Negative word: after the verb it needs no before it, and Spanish keeps both (no veo nada = I don’t see anything)
También: too, also; tampoco: not … either (yo tampoco = me neither)
Courtesy: por favor (please; porfa is the casual short form), gracias (thanks), de nada (you’re welcome), perdón / lo siento (sorry)
Al = a + el, del = de + el (always written as one word)
The: el (masculine), la (feminine), los, las (plural); it matches its noun
A, an: un (masculine), una (feminine); unos, unas = some
Lo que: what, the thing that (lo que dices = what you say)
Lo + adjective: the … thing, the … part (lo bueno = the good thing)
El que, la que: the one who, the one that
Possessive: mi (my), tu (your), su (his, her, its, their, or your with usted); it matches the thing owned
This and that: este (near me), ese (near you), aquel (far from both); esto, eso = this, that (thing)
Mío, tuyo, suyo: mine, yours, his or hers; after the noun or alone (un amigo mío, el tuyo)
Otro: another, other (never un otro)
Todo: all, every, everything (todo el día = all day; todos los días = every day)
Cada: each, every (cada día); it never changes its form
Algo, alguien, algún: something, someone, some (their negatives are nada, nadie, ningún)
Quantity: poco (little, few), un poco (a little), demasiado (too much), bastante (enough, quite), varios (several), tanto (so much)
Muy: very (+ adjective or adverb); mucho: a lot, much, many (+ noun or verb)
Comparison: más … que = more … than; menos … que = less … than (más de + number)
Como (no accent): like, as (como tú = like you), or since at the start (como llovía, = since it was raining)
Tan … como: as … as; tanto como = as much as
Superlative: el / la más … = the most …; el / la menos … = the least …
Mejor (better), peor (worse), mayor (older, bigger), menor (younger, smaller)
-ísimo: extremely (buenísimo = really good)
Por: because of, through, by, along; for in exchange or for a part of the day (gracias por…, por la mañana)
Para + infinitive: in order to
Para: for (a person, a purpose, a deadline), towards
A: to (a place), at (a time); also before a person who is the object (veo a María)
En: in, on, at; by (en coche = by car)
De: of, from; ’s (el libro de Ana = Ana’s book)
Con: with (conmigo = with me, contigo = with you)
Sin: without (sin + infinitive = without doing)
Desde: from, since; hasta: until, as far as, even (¡hasta luego! = see you later)
Entre (between, among), sobre (on, about), hacia (towards), durante (during), según (according to), contra (against)
Antes de / después de + infinitive: before / after doing
Al + infinitive: when, on doing (al llegar = when I arrived)
Y: and (e before a word starting with an i sound: padres e hijos)
O: or (u before a word starting with an o sound: siete u ocho)
Ni: nor, not even (ni tú ni yo = neither you nor I; no tengo ni idea = I have no idea)
Pero: but
Sino: but rather (after no: no es rojo, sino azul)
Porque: because (+ sentence)
So, that’s why (así que, por eso, entonces)
Mientras: while; mientras tanto = meanwhile
Hace + time: ago (hace tres años = three years ago)
Desde hace + time: for, still going on (vivo aquí desde hace dos años = I’ve lived here for two years)
Ya: already, now (ya no = not anymore); todavía, aún: still (todavía no = not yet)
Cada vez más: more and more (cada vez menos = less and less)
How often: siempre (always), a menudo (often), a veces (sometimes), de vez en cuando (now and then)
Usted: polite you, with the él / ella verb form (usted habla); ustedes: you all
Subject pronoun: often left out, since the verb ending shows the person (hablo = I speak); said for emphasis or contrast
Mí, ti: yo and tú after a preposition (para mí, sin ti; but conmigo, contigo)
Vosotros: you all, informal (Spain); Latin America says ustedes
Vos: informal you in Argentina, Uruguay and parts of Central America (vos sabés = tú sabes)
Que: who, which, that (adds a description to a noun)
Que: that (creo que… = I think that…); English often leaves it out
Quien: who, whom (after a preposition or comma: con quien = with whom)
Donde (no accent): where, the place where
Cuyo: whose (it matches the thing owned: cuya casa)
Present: what happens now, usually, or soon (como = I eat, I’m eating)
Preterite: a finished action at a set time in the past (ayer comí = I ate yesterday)
Imperfect: background, habits or something going on in the past (comía = I used to eat, I was eating)
Future: will do; also a guess about now (será él = it must be him)
Conditional: would do; also polite requests (¿podrías…? = could you…?)
Present subjunctive: after wishes, feelings, doubts, purposes and a future “when” (quiero que vengas)
Imperfect subjunctive: the subjunctive in the past, and unreal ifs (si tuviera = if I had)
Command: tells someone to do something (habla = speak!)
Negative command: no + subjunctive (no hables = don’t speak)
Gerund (-ando / -iendo): doing, by doing (with estar: happening now)
Past participle (-ado / -ido): done; after haber, and as an adjective (cansado = tired)
Infinitive: the verb\'s dictionary form (-ar, -er, -ir), used after another verb or a preposition (para comer, sin hablar)
No: not; it goes before the verb (and before me, te, lo…)
Object pronoun before the verb: lo, la (it, him, her), le (to him, to her), me, te, nos (me, you, us)
Reflexive: the action is done to yourself (me llamo = I call myself, my name is; se levanta = he gets up)
Se: people in general, or a passive (se habla español = Spanish is spoken)
Se lo: le becomes se before lo, la, los, las (se lo di = I gave it to him)
Se me…: something happened to me by accident (se me olvidó = I forgot; se me cayó = I dropped it)
Pronouns joined to the end: after a command, an infinitive or a gerund (dámelo = give it to me)
If: a real or likely condition (si llueve, no salgo = if it rains, I won’t go out)
If: unreal or unlikely now (si tuviera dinero, viajaría = if I had money, I would travel)
If: an unreal past (si hubiera sabido = if I had known)
Si after know or ask: whether (no sé si viene = I don’t know whether he’s coming)
Cuando: when (cuándo, with an accent, asks a question)
Cuando + subjunctive: when, for something that hasn’t happened yet (cuando llegues = when you arrive)
Aunque: although, even though
Aunque + subjunctive: even if
Es que: the thing is…, it’s just that… (gives an excuse or explanation)
Conversation word: fills or steers the talk (vale = okay, bueno = well, pues = well / so, venga = come on, a ver = let’s see, o sea = I mean)
